source_text: De tempore uero non erit otiosa extrinsecus obseruatio etiam horarum quarundam, istarum dico communium quae diei interspatia signant, tertia, sexta, nona; quas sollemniores in scripturis inuenire est. primus spiritus sanctus congregatis discipulis hora tertia infusus est. Petrus, qua die uisionem communitatis omnis in illo uasculo expertus est, sexta hora orandi gratia ascenderat in superiora. idem cum Iohanne ad nonam in templum adibat, ubi paralyticum sanitati reformauit. quae etsi simpliciter se habent sine ullius obseruationis praecepto, bonum tamen sit aliquam constituere praesumptionem, quae et orandi admonitionem constringat et quasi lege ad tale munus extorqueat a negotiis interdum, ut, quod Danieli quoque legimus obseruatum utique ex Israelis disciplina, ne minus ter die saltem adoremus, debitores trium Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti; exceptis utique legitimis orationibus, quae sine ulla admonitione debentur ingressu lucis et noctis. sed et cibum non prius sumere et lauacrum non prius adire quam interposita oratione fideles decet. priora enim habenda sunt spiritus refrigeria et pabula quam carnis, quia priora caelestia quam terrena.
thought_title: Times of Prayer and the Priority of Spiritual Refreshment
orientation: Tertullian is giving practical instruction on the times and customs of Christian prayer, after expounding the Lord's Prayer itself.
pass_a_gloss: But about the time, the outward observance of certain hours will not be idle, I mean those common ones which mark the intervals of the day, the third, the sixth, the ninth; which are found in the scriptures as more solemn. First, the Holy Spirit was poured upon the disciples gathered together at the third hour. Peter, on the day on which he experienced the vision of the community of all things in that vessel, had gone up to the upper parts at the sixth hour for the sake of praying. The same man with John was going into the temple at the ninth hour, where he restored the paralytic to health. Even if these things stand simply, without any precept of observance, nevertheless it would be good to establish some presumption, which both binds the reminder of praying and, as if by a law, extorts such a duty from business affairs from time to time, so that, what we read was also observed by Daniel certainly from the teaching of Israel, we may adore at least not less than three times a day, debtors of the three, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; excepting certainly the lawful prayers, which are owed without any reminder at the entering of light and of night. But also it is fitting for the faithful not to take food earlier and not to go to the bath earlier than with prayer placed in between. For the refreshments and nourishments of the spirit are to be held before those of the flesh, because heavenly things are before earthly things.

choices.why: Keeps the legal-rhetorical sense of a settled prior claim or practice that constrains behavior, matching Tertullian's argument that a custom can bind without a formal precept.
Preserves the forceful, almost violent metaphor Tertullian uses for how a fixed custom pulls one away from business to prayer.
Renders the concrete noun Tertullian uses for spiritual comfort, keeping the parallel with food and bath refreshment of the body.
Keeps the feeding metaphor for what sustains the spirit, parallel to food for the flesh.
Preserves the theological point that Christians owe worship to each person of the Trinity, not just to God generally.

bible_refs.note: The Holy Spirit poured out on the disciples at the third hour.
Peter went up to pray at the sixth hour and saw the vision of the vessel.
Peter and John going up to the temple at the ninth hour, where the paralytic was healed.
Daniel observed prayer three times a day according to Israelite teaching.

pass_b_english: As for the time of prayer, it will not be useless to observe also certain hours outwardly. I mean the common hours that mark the intervals of the day: the third, the sixth, and the ninth. We find these treated as more solemn in the Scriptures. The Holy Spirit was first poured out upon the gathered disciples at the third hour (Acts 2:1-4). Peter, on the day he experienced the vision of the community of all things in that vessel, had gone up to the upper room at the sixth hour to pray (Acts 10:9). The same Peter, with John, was going up to the temple at the ninth hour, where he restored the paralytic to health (Acts 3:1). These examples stand simply as they are, without any command to observe them. Still, it would be good to establish some settled practice. Such a practice both binds us to the reminder to pray and, as if by a law, sometimes drags us away from our business to this duty. Then, as we read Daniel also observed, certainly from Israelite teaching, we may worship no less than three times a day at least, as debtors of the three: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Daniel 6:10). This is of course in addition to the regular prayers that are owed without any reminder at the coming of light and of night. It is also fitting for believers not to take food or go to the bath before prayer has been set in between. For the refreshments and nourishments of the spirit must come before those of the flesh, because heavenly things come before earthly things.

problems.source_quote: primus spiritus sanctus congregatis discipulis hora tertia infusus est.
problems.why: The pouring out of the Holy Spirit at the third hour is recorded in Acts 2:1‑4, not Acts 2:15.
problems.fix: The Holy Spirit was first poured out upon the gathered disciples at the third hour (Acts 2:1‑4).
problems.ruling: Acts 2:15 mentions the third hour; the Spirit's pouring is Acts 2:1-4, so the reference misleads readers.

fixed: The pouring out of the Holy Spirit at the third hour is recorded in Acts 2:1-4, not Acts 2:15.

polish.changed: Clarified the hours as common daily markers, broke long sentences into natural modern units, made the implied subject of the practice explicit, and smoothed the rhythm for reading aloud while preserving every claim and Scripture reference.

notes.quote: the third, the sixth, and the ninth
notes.why: Hours of prayer not explained as Roman time (9 AM, noon, 3 PM).
